full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, C. J.-This application is directed against the judgment and order dated 20th August, 1974 passed by the Labor Court, Khulna in Miscellaneous Case No. 34 of 1974 (LR.O. Case No. 629 of 1973 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, dismissing the case. 

 3. Before we take up the above noted points for consideration it appears that it would be pertinent to take up for consideration the basic question involved in this case, namely, whether the Labor Court is a Civil Court within the meaning of the Code of Civil Procedure and is competent to entertain application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 4. Mr. Niazmuddin Haider, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that Labour Court is a Civil Court because, it is clothed with the powers of the Civil Court under section 36 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969. Since the Labor Court functions as a Civil Court, there cannot be any objection to entertain an application under Order IX, rule 13. In support of the above proposition the learned Advocate relies upon a decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of M/s. M. M. Ispahani Vs. Chairman, Second Labor Court and another, (1967) 19 DLR 612. 

 5. From the decision in the case of M/s. M. Ispahani, it appears that a similar question was raised before a Division Bench. The Division Bench has taken the view that the Labor Court trying a complaint under section 25 of the East Pakistan Employment of Labor (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 is a, court of civil jurisdiction; and that such court is a court in accordance with the provision of section 141 of the Code. The learned Judges have answered the question in the affirmative stating that the Labor Court having been empowered under the East Pakistan Labor Disputes Act, 1965 exercises all the jurisdictions of a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure and as such is competent to exercise the Civil Court's power under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 "(2) The Court shall for the purpose of adjudicating and determining any labor dispute and for the purpose of interpreting any award, decision or order, be deemed to be a Civil Court     and shall have the fame powers as are vested in such Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (V of 1908), subject to the provisions of sub-section (1) and shall also have the powers of acting under section 480 of the Cede of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (V of 1898), in cases of contempt. 

 8. From the discussions in the judgment it appears that no argument was advanced before the learned Judges regarding the nature and character of a proceeding under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A proceeding under Order IX rule 13 is an original proceeding, independent of the suit. When a suit is disposed of and decreed exparte, it is revived only after successful termination of as application under Order IX rule 13, that is, after the exparte decree is set aside. Another aspect is that Order IX, rule 13 is only applicable in a case where decree is passed and it is not applicable in a case which ends in an order. In the instant case application under Order IX, rule 13 was filed before the Labor Court in connection with a proceeding under a special statute. In some decisions it has been held that Order IX, rule 13 may be applied to as order passed in an independent proceeding as contemplated under section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But this view cannot be stretched to such an extent to make the provisions of Order IX, rule 13 applicable to a proceeding under the Employment of Labor (Standing Orders) Act, 1965. 

 12. A Tribunal does not become a Civil Court as defined under section 4 of the East Bengal Civil Courts Act of 1887. Civil Court as defined in the said Act does not include any such kind of tribunals as created under the special statute. The view we are taking gets support from the observations made in the case of Bangladesh Fishermen's Co-operative Society Ltd. Vs. The Chairman, Labor Court, Chittagong and another, (1975) 27 DLR 367. In this case the question for consideration was, as to whether a Labor Court constituted under section 36 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 is a Civil Court and attracts the bar contained in section 133 of the Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1940. 

 13. In this case a Division Bench has taken the view that by virtue of clause (2) of section 36 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969. the Labor Court shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for the specified purpose of adjudicating and determining an industrial dispute; and that the use of the word "deemed" in this clause definitely indicates that a Labor Court is not ordinarily a Civil Court, but it shall be considered to be so in respect of the proceedings before it for deciding an industrial dispute.
